From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter

**To:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Re:** Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)
**Status:** Privileged – buyer internal working advice

## Headline view

The Seller's covering note describes the package as "fair and balanced." It is not. Read together, the Seller Update and the Disclosure Letter do two things:

1. **Collapse the protection architecture.** Fundamental/title warranties, tax, IP and the specific indemnities are all pulled under one general regime (20% cap, 18 months, basket/de minimis, exclusive remedy), and the Buyer's knowledge clause (8.3) combined with blanket data-room disclosure (Sch 7 / DL 1.1) would strip out most claims before you reach the cap at all.
2. **Leave every known DD problem unresolved and shift it to the Buyer.** The Disclosure Letter is actually quite candid — it admits that Bluefen consent, Riverlark discharge, Ironquay payment, the bonus funding, and the privacy incident are all *not* resolved — but the Seller Update then treats each one as "addressed," "adequate," "ordinary course," or "not material." The candour in the letter is there to make these matters "disclosed" (and therefore unclaimable), not to fix them.

The most serious single problem is **Riverlark**: a ~AUD 3.2m secured facility, with change-of-control and discharge clauses, where the release is to come *after* Completion. On a debt-free/cash-free deal that is an uncovered price leakage and security risk of ~13% of the purchase price.

Also note: the Disclosure Letter speaks as at **22 September 2026**. It is now 4 November. Nothing in the package confirms the position has not worsened in the intervening six weeks. We should require a bring-down.

---

## Part A – Liability architecture (Clauses 8, 9, 12, 13, 20)

### A1. Fundamental and title warranties subject to general cap and time limit

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties share the 20% cap and 18-month period "for administrative simplicity."

**Why it's a problem:** This is the core of the deal. If the Seller does not own, or cannot transfer, 100% of the shares free of encumbrances, the Buyer loses the entire AUD 24m, not 20% of it. Capping title at AUD 4.8m means the Seller keeps AUD 19.2m for shares it may not have been entitled to sell. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason; it is an acknowledgement that the Seller knows what it's asking for.

Market in Australian private M&A: fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency) capped at 100% of price, time limit typically 6–7 years or at least the longer of statutory limitation and a lengthy period. Leakage/debt-free covenants are usually uncapped or capped at price.

**Push back:** Carve fundamental warranties (and the leakage/debt-free-cash-free covenant) out of 12.1–12.3 entirely. Cap at 100% of price; 6-year claim period (or no limit other than statute). No de minimis/basket.

### A2. "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (12.3 / 13) and "limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance apply to all Claims of any nature" (9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Why it's a problem:** These are drafting devices that make every carve-out you negotiate elsewhere useless unless you also remember to repeat it here. "All Claims of any nature" would sweep in:
- the specific indemnities (Ironquay, privacy incident, bonuses, Riverlark);
- the tax indemnity;
- completion deliverable/covenant breaches;
- fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment;
- the price-adjustment / leakage mechanics.

Capping an indemnity at the same level as a warranty defeats the purpose of having an indemnity. Applying a cap or exclusive-remedy clause to fraud is unenforceable as a matter of policy in any event, but we should not have to litigate that.

**Push back:** Reverse the default. The limitations in cl. 12 apply only to general Warranty Claims. Express carve-outs: fundamental warranties, tax warranties/indemnity, specific indemnities, leakage/debt-free covenant, completion obligations, fraud/wilful misconduct, and any claim under the Australian Consumer Law to the extent it cannot be excluded.

### A3. General cap (20%), basket (AUD 250k), de minimis (AUD 25k), 18 months

Taken alone these are within a defensible range for general warranties on a AUD 24m deal, but:
- **"Only the excess above the basket is recoverable"** – this is a deductible, not a tipping basket. Ask for a tipping (first-dollar) basket at ~1% (AUD 240k). If the Seller holds on deductible, trade for a lower threshold (AUD 120k) and lower cap-side concessions elsewhere.
- **18 months** – short. Buyer will typically not have been through a full audit cycle plus follow-up on an 18-month clock. Ask for 24 months for general warranties; for tax, the longer of 7 years and the period for the ATO to amend an assessment plus a few months.
- **20% cap** – acceptable on the general book *only* if the known problems (Part B) are dealt with by specific indemnities or price adjustments outside the cap. If the Seller insists everything sits under the cap, the cap must rise materially (30–40%) or a retention/escrow must cover the known exposures.

### A4. Clause 8.3 – Buyer knowledge, including anything "discoverable" from data room or public records

**Why it's a problem:** As drafted this is not a knowledge qualifier; it is a release. "Discoverable" is constructive knowledge — the Seller would argue any matter that *could* have been found in any document in the data room or any ASIC/PPSR/court search is barred, whether or not anyone actually found it or understood it. Combined with DL [1.1] (blanket disclosure of "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room), the Seller's position is that the warranties are qualified by the entire data room *and* that anything in the data room cannot be claimed on anyway. The warranties become almost ornamental.

Also note "or its advisers" — the Seller would impute the knowledge of every lawyer, accountant and technical adviser who touched the data room.

**Push back:**
- Delete 8.3, or limit it to *actual* knowledge of a short, named list of Buyer deal-team individuals, and only where the matter was "fairly disclosed" (see A5).
- Delete "discoverable" and "public records" entirely.
- Make clear that the Buyer's DD does not reduce the Seller's liability (standard "no diminution" clause).

### A5. Disclosure standard (Schedule 7 / DL 1.1–1.2, 1.4)

**Why it's a problem:** General disclosure of the whole data room and "publicly searchable corporate records" is not a disclosure standard the Buyer should accept. The test should be *fair disclosure* — disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. A 400-document data room is not fair disclosure of a single clause buried in one of them.

Clause [1.4] ("nothing admits … that any consent, payment, notice … is legally required") is designed to let the Seller say in future: "we disclosed it, so you can't claim; but we never admitted it was a problem, so we have no obligation to fix it." That is the worst of both worlds for the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Replace general data-room disclosure with: (i) the specific disclosures in the Disclosure Letter, and (ii) only those data-room documents specifically referenced against the relevant warranty, each fairly disclosed.
- Public register disclosure limited to a short list of named searches on named dates (ASIC company search, PPSR against the Company's ABN/ACN, court searches), with the search results annexed.
- Strike [1.4] or amend so that it does not operate to deny the Seller's obligations under the SPA (consents, discharges, indemnities).
- Require a bring-down disclosure letter at Completion, with no new disclosures permitted against the warranties for matters arising between signing and Completion (those are the Seller's risk, giving rise to a termination right / price adjustment rather than mere "disclosure").

---

## Part B – Known DD issues the Seller has left unresolved

The Disclosure Letter is useful because it tells us, in the Seller's own words, what has **not** been done. Each should be a condition precedent, a Completion deliverable, a price adjustment, or a specific indemnity outside the cap — and in some cases all of them.

### B1. Riverlark Bank facility (~AUD 3.2m) — *highest priority*

**Seller position:** Release "to be provided following Completion."
**Disclosure Letter:** Facility NOT repaid; no discharge of security; change-of-control (8.1) and discharge (9.2) clauses on file.

**Why it's a problem:**
- Debt-free/cash-free means the Buyer pays AUD 24m for an enterprise with no debt. If AUD 3.2m is still outstanding at Completion and secured over the Company, the Buyer has overpaid by AUD 3.2m and the Company's assets are encumbered.
- The change-of-control clause (8.1) will almost certainly be triggered by the share sale — meaning the bank can call the facility and enforce security against *the Buyer's* new subsidiary on day one.
- A "release following Completion" is a promise from a seller who by then has the money. If the Seller does not procure it, the Buyer's recourse is a damages claim — which under the Seller's cl. 12 drafting would be capped, time-barred and subject to the basket.
- No evidence the bank has consented to the change of control.

**Push back:**
- Repayment of Riverlark and delivery of a signed deed of release, PPSR discharge, and ASIC Form 312 (or equivalent) are **Completion deliverables**; alternatively, repay from the purchase price at Completion via the funds flow, with a bank payout letter obtained pre-Completion stating the exact payout figure and confirming release on receipt.
- Bank consent to change of control (if the Seller wants the facility to survive, which the Buyer should not want) as a CP.
- Debt-free/cash-free adjustment: any amount outstanding at Completion is deducted dollar-for-dollar from the price.
- Uncapped indemnity for any amount or cost arising from the facility or security not being discharged at Completion.

### B2. Bluefen change-of-control consent (~AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30% of FY26)

**Seller position:** "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours; condition satisfied on delivery of counterparty's written consent.
**Disclosure Letter:** No final written consent; no evidence the conditions in cl. 11.3 are satisfied.

**Why it's a problem:**
- This is the Company's largest customer. Losing it post-Completion would wipe out close to a third of revenue; the purchase price was presumably built on a multiple of that revenue.
- "Reasonable endeavours" is a low standard; the Seller can say it tried.
- The CP as drafted is satisfied on delivery of "written consent" — but DD-002 cl. 11.3 attaches *conditions* to consent. A conditional consent, or a consent given subject to re-pricing or termination rights, would technically satisfy the Seller's CP while leaving the Buyer exposed.
- "Addressed" is not a legal status.

**Push back:**
- CP: Bluefen's written, **unconditional** consent (or written confirmation that all 11.3 conditions are satisfied), in a form approved by the Buyer, not revocable, with no amendment to pricing or term. Seller obligation: *best* endeavours; Buyer to be kept informed and to have a right to attend/participate in discussions.
- Buyer-only waiver right; long-stop date.
- Fall-back if the Seller won't accept the CP: price adjustment / deferred consideration tied to Bluefen retention for 12 months post-Completion, plus specific indemnity for loss if Bluefen terminates or re-prices on the basis of change of control.
- Request the current status now — the letter is six weeks old.

### B3. Ironquay IP — Statement of Work 3 (AUD 180k open)

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment is "adequate."
**Disclosure Letter:** IP in SOW3 project materials only transfers on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee; DD-010 shows AUD 180k unpaid; no receipt, no confirmatory assignment on file; and the Seller volunteers that DD-010 is "not independent bank verification of non-payment" (i.e. it might be *more* unpaid, or paid — they don't know).

**Why it's a problem:**
- The issue is not the AUD 180k. The issue is that **the Company may not own the IP in whatever SOW3 built**, and we do not know what that is. If it is part of the analytics platform the Buyer is paying AUD 24m for, this is a title-to-assets problem, not a payables problem.
- An indemnity capped at the fee covers the cost of paying Ironquay, but not: the cost if Ironquay refuses to assign, raises its price, asserts licence terms, or has already licensed the materials elsewhere; business interruption; or re-development cost.
- The Seller's own drafting of cl. 12 would sweep this "existing indemnity" under the 20% cap and 18-month limit (see A2).

**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion: the Seller to pay the AUD 180k (and anything else outstanding), obtain a receipt, and deliver a **confirmatory deed of assignment** from Ironquay of all SOW1–3 project materials and IP, plus moral rights consents from Ironquay personnel — as Completion deliverables.
- Confirm in DD exactly what SOW3 delivered and whether it is in the production codebase.
- Specific indemnity (outside cap, 6 years): all loss arising from any Ironquay IP not vesting in the Company at Completion, including cost of acquiring, licensing or re-developing it.
- Extend IP warranties: Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business; no third party has any claim; all contractor IP assigned in writing.

### B4. Completion bonuses (AUD 420k) not in the funds flow

**Seller position:** "A matter for the Seller," not itemised.
**Disclosure Letter:** AUD 420k in Completion bonuses conditional on Completion and continued employment; not in the funds flow; silent on payroll tax, super and on-costs.

**Why it's a problem:**
- These are transaction bonuses **payable by the Company**, triggered by Completion. If not paid or funded at Completion, the Company (now the Buyer's) pays them. That is classic "transaction cost leakage" on a debt-free/cash-free deal.
- Payroll tax (NSW: 5.45%), superannuation (12% SG for FY27) and any related on-costs could add roughly AUD 70–75k, so the true number is closer to AUD 490–500k.
- "Continued employment" condition — if paid post-Completion, the Buyer may become the party bound to keep those employees on, or face claims if they leave.
- "A matter for the Seller" is the correct outcome, but it has to be *in the document*: an unitemised oral assurance is worth nothing.

**Push back:**
- Treat bonuses plus all on-costs as Transaction Expenses / debt-like items deducted from the price, or paid by the Seller at Completion through the funds flow with evidence.
- Specific indemnity (uncapped) for any bonus, on-cost or claim arising from DD-005 arrangements.
- Obtain the bonus letters; check who the recipients are (if they are key staff, think about retention arrangements the Buyer *does* want, separately funded).

### B5. Export / privacy incident (DD-006, ~1,240 records)

**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter," not expected to be material.
**Disclosure Letter:** Download link sent to an unintended external email address; ~1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps; unknown whether accessed; unknown scope; unknown whether notification required; investigation "preliminary" as at 22 September.

**Why it's a problem:**
- Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires assessment within 30 days of a suspected eligible data breach. The incident was disclosed as "preliminary" on 22 September; it is now 4 November. Either the assessment has been done (and the Seller should tell us the outcome) or the Company is already outside the statutory assessment window. Both matter.
- The data appears to be customer data (names/roles/activity timestamps of a B2B analytics company's users). If any of it is Bluefen's or Mossvale's data, there are likely contractual notification and security obligations under those customer contracts, and reputational/termination risk.
- Post-December 2022 amendments, maximum civil penalties for serious interference with privacy are the greater of AUD 50m, 3× benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover. "Not expected to be material" is the Seller's hope, not an assessment.
- Characterising it as "not a confirmed breach" and "no loss amount" is positioning for a later argument that the warranty was not breached and the loss was unforeseeable.

**Push back:**
- Immediate DD request: status of investigation, whether the recipient confirmed deletion/non-access, whether the OAIC or affected individuals/customers were notified, whose data it was, and copies of any legal advice (or at minimum a factual summary).
- Specific indemnity, outside cap, 6 years: all loss, fines, notification costs, remediation, customer claims and contractual consequences arising from DD-006.
- Warranty that the Company has complied with the Privacy Act and APPs and has no unnotified eligible data breaches, *not* qualified by DD-006 disclosure.
- Consider a CP or pre-Completion covenant requiring the Seller to complete the assessment and make any required notifications before Completion, with Buyer approval of communications.

### B6. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.
**Disclosure Letter:** Three *related* renewals to be read together for timing and scope; the Seller does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Why it's a problem:** Three identical AUD 110k contracts with the same supplier, to be "read together," looks like a single AUD 330k commitment split to stay under an approval or disclosure threshold. Questions: Are they signed? Are they pre-Completion commitments that bind the Company for a new term? Are the amounts accrued (debt-like) or future opex? Are they related-party in any way? Is Sandbar a necessary supplier?

**Push back:** Get the three documents and the commercial rationale. If renewals were entered into after the locked-box date / outside the ordinary course, treat as leakage. Pre-Completion conduct covenant: no new or renewed commitments above a threshold (say AUD 50k) without Buyer consent, and no splitting of commitments. If the Buyer does not need Sandbar, require termination pre-Completion or price adjustment.

### B7. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)

- **Lease:** The Seller says it is a "notification" not a consent. Fine — but then the notification should be given pre-Completion and evidence delivered at Completion. Confirm landlord has not objected and the lease has no change-of-control termination right.
- **Mossvale:** The letter says restriction on assignment, not consent on share sale. Accept provisionally, but verify the clause ourselves (change-of-control clauses are often drafted as "assignment includes change in control"). Warranty that no customer or supplier contract contains a change-of-control right other than as disclosed, with a list.

### B8. Title (DD-012)

**Seller position:** Title evidenced by the Company's own share register.
**Disclosure Letter:** The register is "the source relied on"; Buyer has not completed its own verification.

**Why it's a problem:** A company's share register is maintained by the company (i.e. by the Seller's own people). It is evidence of registration, not of beneficial ownership or absence of encumbrances. The Seller is simultaneously (i) relying on this as the sole title evidence and (ii) seeking to cap the title warranty at 20% and 18 months (A1). We should not accept both.

**Push back:** ASIC extract; PPSR search against the Company and the Seller (for security over the shares — Riverlark may have a share mortgage); share certificates; copies of any shareholder agreements, options, convertible notes, employee equity. Fundamental warranties on title: legal and beneficial owner, free of all Encumbrances, no options or rights to subscribe. Uncapped, 6 years (per A1).

### B9. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

Not acceptable. Tax: separate uncapped (or price-capped) tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, with a claim period tied to the ATO amendment period; the Seller controls nothing after Completion. IP: given Ironquay (B3), IP warranties need to be at least a higher cap and longer period (3–4 years), and the ownership warranty should sit with fundamentals.

---

## Part C – Points of general positioning

- **Stale date.** All disclosures speak at 22 September 2026. Require updated disclosure now and a formal bring-down at Completion. Any deterioration between now and Completion is for the Seller.
- **Non-reliance (20.5).** Non-reliance on representations outside the SPA is standard; non-reliance that extends to the warranties themselves, or that purports to exclude liability for misleading conduct under the ACL/ASIC Act for fraud, is not. Limit to pre-contractual statements and carve out fraud and non-excludable statutory liability.
- **Exclusive remedy (12.8).** Acceptable for general warranty damages. Must not exclude: rescission for fraud, specific performance of Completion obligations, injunctive relief, the price-adjustment and leakage mechanics, or statutory rights that cannot be excluded.
- **Retention / escrow.** Given the number of unresolved items and a Seller that wants post-Completion "releases" and "reasonable endeavours," a retention of **AUD 2.4–3.6m (10–15%)** held for 18–24 months is justified, releasable against resolution of Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-006 and Bluefen. If the Seller resists on the basis that it is a clean-skin seller, the alternative is to fix every item pre-Completion as CPs/deliverables.
- **Seller covenant strength.** Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd — a "Ventures" vehicle may distribute proceeds immediately post-Completion. Diligence its covenant; consider a parent guarantee or the retention above. A good indemnity against an empty shell is worth nothing.
- **W&I insurance.** If the Seller's attitude to caps is immovable, W&I could bridge the gap on the general warranty book — but insurers will exclude all the known matters in Part B. Those still need specific indemnities or price fixes from the Seller.

---

## Summary of recommendations (priority order)

| # | Issue | Recommended Buyer position |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Riverlark AUD 3.2m facility** | Repay and deliver signed release / PPSR discharge **at** Completion via funds flow and payout letter; dollar-for-dollar price deduction for any debt remaining; uncapped indemnity. Not post-Completion. |
| 2 | **Fundamental / title warranties** | Carve out of cl. 12 entirely. Cap at 100% of price; 6 years; no basket/de minimis. Title evidence: ASIC, PPSR (Company and Seller), certificates, cap table docs — not just the register. |
| 3 | **"All Claims of any nature" drafting (12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5)** | Reverse the default: limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims. Express carve-outs for fundamentals, tax, specific indemnities, leakage, completion obligations, fraud, non-excludable statutory liability. |
| 4 | **Bluefen consent** | CP: unconditional written consent in Buyer-approved form, with 11.3 conditions satisfied; best endeavours; Buyer-only waiver. Fallback: deferred consideration / indemnity tied to retention. Confirm current status. |
| 5 | **Cl. 8.3 Buyer knowledge + general data-room disclosure** | Delete constructive/"discoverable" knowledge and adviser imputation; actual knowledge of named individuals only, and only of fairly disclosed matters. Replace blanket disclosure with fair-disclosure standard and specifically referenced documents. Strike or neutralise DL [1.4]. Bring-down disclosure letter with no new disclosures against warranties. |
| 6 | **Ironquay SOW3 IP** | Seller pays all outstanding fees and delivers confirmatory assignment + moral rights consents as Completion deliverables; uncapped specific indemnity for IP not vesting; confirm what SOW3 built. |
| 7 | **DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs ≈ AUD 490–500k)** | Treat as transaction expense/debt-like item deducted from price or paid by Seller through the funds flow with evidence; uncapped indemnity. |
| 8 | **DD-006 privacy incident** | Immediate status update (NDB assessment window has likely run); specific uncapped indemnity, 6 years; unqualified privacy-compliance warranty; pre-Completion covenant to complete assessment and notifications with Buyer sign-off. |
| 9 | **Tax / IP regimes** | Separate tax indemnity (price-capped or uncapped, ATO amendment period + buffer). IP warranties: higher cap, 3–4 years; ownership with fundamentals. |
| 10 | **General regime numbers** | Tipping basket at ~1% (not deductible); general claims period 24 months; 20% cap acceptable only if known matters sit outside it — otherwise 30–40% or retention. |
| 11 | **Sandbar renewals** | Obtain documents; treat as leakage if outside ordinary course/post-locked-box; pre-Completion conduct covenant with AUD 50k threshold and anti-splitting language. |
| 12 | **Lease / Mossvale** | Notification given pre-Completion with evidence; verify Mossvale clause ourselves; warranty listing all change-of-control provisions. |
| 13 | **Retention / covenant** | 10–15% retention for 18–24 months released against resolution of items 1, 4, 6, 8; diligence Seller covenant strength; consider guarantee. W&I only as a supplement, not a substitute, for the known issues. |
| 14 | **Timing** | Require refreshed disclosure immediately (current letter is six weeks stale) and formal bring-down at Completion. |

**Overall negotiating posture:** The Seller's package offers general-warranty-level protection for fundamental-level risks, and asks the Buyer to inherit ~AUD 3.6m of debt and bonus leakage on a debt-free/cash-free price, plus unresolved IP title and privacy exposure, with an 18-month, 20%-capped claim as the only recourse. Our mark-up should re-separate fundamentals, indemnities and tax from the general regime, convert every "to be provided after Completion" into a Completion deliverable or price deduction, and replace blanket disclosure with fair disclosure. These are not aggressive positions; they are the ordinary allocation of known risks to the party that created them and controls their resolution.

Happy to turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up of the SPA and a response letter to Seller's counsel, and to draft the DD requisition list (Bluefen status, Riverlark payout letter, Ironquay deliverables, bonus letters, DD-006 investigation outcome, Sandbar contracts, PPSR/ASIC searches).

# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter

**To:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Re:** Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)
**Status:** Privileged – buyer internal working advice

## Headline view

The Seller's covering note describes the package as "fair and balanced." It is not. Read together, the Seller Update and the Disclosure Letter do two things:

1. **Collapse the protection architecture.** Fundamental/title warranties, tax, IP and the specific indemnities are all pulled under one general regime (20% cap, 18 months, basket/de minimis, exclusive remedy), and the Buyer's knowledge clause (8.3) combined with blanket data-room disclosure (Sch 7 / DL 1.1) would strip out most claims before you reach the cap at all.
2. **Leave every known DD problem unresolved and shift it to the Buyer.** The Disclosure Letter is actually quite candid — it admits that Bluefen consent, Riverlark discharge, Ironquay payment, the bonus funding, and the privacy incident are all *not* resolved — but the Seller Update then treats each one as "addressed," "adequate," "ordinary course," or "not material." The candour in the letter is there to make these matters "disclosed" (and therefore unclaimable), not to fix them.

The most serious single problem is **Riverlark**: a ~AUD 3.2m secured facility, with change-of-control and discharge clauses, where the release is to come *after* Completion. On a debt-free/cash-free deal that is an uncovered price leakage and security risk of ~13% of the purchase price.

Also note: the Disclosure Letter speaks as at **22 September 2026**. It is now 4 November. Nothing in the package confirms the position has not worsened in the intervening six weeks. We should require a bring-down.

---

## Part A – Liability architecture (Clauses 8, 9, 12, 13, 20)

### A1. Fundamental and title warranties subject to general cap and time limit

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties share the 20% cap and 18-month period "for administrative simplicity."

**Why it's a problem:** This is the core of the deal. If the Seller does not own, or cannot transfer, 100% of the shares free of encumbrances, the Buyer loses the entire AUD 24m, not 20% of it. Capping title at AUD 4.8m means the Seller keeps AUD 19.2m for shares it may not have been entitled to sell. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason; it is an acknowledgement that the Seller knows what it's asking for.

Market in Australian private M&A: fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency) capped at 100% of price, time limit typically 6–7 years or at least the longer of statutory limitation and a lengthy period. Leakage/debt-free covenants are usually uncapped or capped at price.

**Push back:** Carve fundamental warranties (and the leakage/debt-free-cash-free covenant) out of 12.1–12.3 entirely. Cap at 100% of price; 6-year claim period (or no limit other than statute). No de minimis/basket.

### A2. "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (12.3 / 13) and "limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance apply to all Claims of any nature" (9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Why it's a problem:** These are drafting devices that make every carve-out you negotiate elsewhere useless unless you also remember to repeat it here. "All Claims of any nature" would sweep in:
- the specific indemnities (Ironquay, privacy incident, bonuses, Riverlark);
- the tax indemnity;
- completion deliverable/covenant breaches;
- fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment;
- the price-adjustment / leakage mechanics.

Capping an indemnity at the same level as a warranty defeats the purpose of having an indemnity. Applying a cap or exclusive-remedy clause to fraud is unenforceable as a matter of policy in any event, but we should not have to litigate that.

**Push back:** Reverse the default. The limitations in cl. 12 apply only to general Warranty Claims. Express carve-outs: fundamental warranties, tax warranties/indemnity, specific indemnities, leakage/debt-free covenant, completion obligations, fraud/wilful misconduct, and any claim under the Australian Consumer Law to the extent it cannot be excluded.

### A3. General cap (20%), basket (AUD 250k), de minimis (AUD 25k), 18 months

Taken alone these are within a defensible range for general warranties on a AUD 24m deal, but:
- **"Only the excess above the basket is recoverable"** – this is a deductible, not a tipping basket. Ask for a tipping (first-dollar) basket at ~1% (AUD 240k). If the Seller holds on deductible, trade for a lower threshold (AUD 120k) and lower cap-side concessions elsewhere.
- **18 months** – short. Buyer will typically not have been through a full audit cycle plus follow-up on an 18-month clock. Ask for 24 months for general warranties; for tax, the longer of 7 years and the period for the ATO to amend an assessment plus a few months.
- **20% cap** – acceptable on the general book *only* if the known problems (Part B) are dealt with by specific indemnities or price adjustments outside the cap. If the Seller insists everything sits under the cap, the cap must rise materially (30–40%) or a retention/escrow must cover the known exposures.

### A4. Clause 8.3 – Buyer knowledge, including anything "discoverable" from data room or public records

**Why it's a problem:** As drafted this is not a knowledge qualifier; it is a release. "Discoverable" is constructive knowledge — the Seller would argue any matter that *could* have been found in any document in the data room or any ASIC/PPSR/court search is barred, whether or not anyone actually found it or understood it. Combined with DL [1.1] (blanket disclosure of "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room), the Seller's position is that the warranties are qualified by the entire data room *and* that anything in the data room cannot be claimed on anyway. The warranties become almost ornamental.

Also note "or its advisers" — the Seller would impute the knowledge of every lawyer, accountant and technical adviser who touched the data room.

**Push back:**
- Delete 8.3, or limit it to *actual* knowledge of a short, named list of Buyer deal-team individuals, and only where the matter was "fairly disclosed" (see A5).
- Delete "discoverable" and "public records" entirely.
- Make clear that the Buyer's DD does not reduce the Seller's liability (standard "no diminution" clause).

### A5. Disclosure standard (Schedule 7 / DL 1.1–1.2, 1.4)

**Why it's a problem:** General disclosure of the whole data room and "publicly searchable corporate records" is not a disclosure standard the Buyer should accept. The test should be *fair disclosure* — disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. A 400-document data room is not fair disclosure of a single clause buried in one of them.

Clause [1.4] ("nothing admits … that any consent, payment, notice … is legally required") is designed to let the Seller say in future: "we disclosed it, so you can't claim; but we never admitted it was a problem, so we have no obligation to fix it." That is the worst of both worlds for the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Replace general data-room disclosure with: (i) the specific disclosures in the Disclosure Letter, and (ii) only those data-room documents specifically referenced against the relevant warranty, each fairly disclosed.
- Public register disclosure limited to a short list of named searches on named dates (ASIC company search, PPSR against the Company's ABN/ACN, court searches), with the search results annexed.
- Strike [1.4] or amend so that it does not operate to deny the Seller's obligations under the SPA (consents, discharges, indemnities).
- Require a bring-down disclosure letter at Completion, with no new disclosures permitted against the warranties for matters arising between signing and Completion (those are the Seller's risk, giving rise to a termination right / price adjustment rather than mere "disclosure").

---

## Part B – Known DD issues the Seller has left unresolved

The Disclosure Letter is useful because it tells us, in the Seller's own words, what has **not** been done. Each should be a condition precedent, a Completion deliverable, a price adjustment, or a specific indemnity outside the cap — and in some cases all of them.

### B1. Riverlark Bank facility (~AUD 3.2m) — *highest priority*

**Seller position:** Release "to be provided following Completion."
**Disclosure Letter:** Facility NOT repaid; no discharge of security; change-of-control (8.1) and discharge (9.2) clauses on file.

**Why it's a problem:**
- Debt-free/cash-free means the Buyer pays AUD 24m for an enterprise with no debt. If AUD 3.2m is still outstanding at Completion and secured over the Company, the Buyer has overpaid by AUD 3.2m and the Company's assets are encumbered.
- The change-of-control clause (8.1) will almost certainly be triggered by the share sale — meaning the bank can call the facility and enforce security against *the Buyer's* new subsidiary on day one.
- A "release following Completion" is a promise from a seller who by then has the money. If the Seller does not procure it, the Buyer's recourse is a damages claim — which under the Seller's cl. 12 drafting would be capped, time-barred and subject to the basket.
- No evidence the bank has consented to the change of control.

**Push back:**
- Repayment of Riverlark and delivery of a signed deed of release, PPSR discharge, and ASIC Form 312 (or equivalent) are **Completion deliverables**; alternatively, repay from the purchase price at Completion via the funds flow, with a bank payout letter obtained pre-Completion stating the exact payout figure and confirming release on receipt.
- Bank consent to change of control (if the Seller wants the facility to survive, which the Buyer should not want) as a CP.
- Debt-free/cash-free adjustment: any amount outstanding at Completion is deducted dollar-for-dollar from the price.
- Uncapped indemnity for any amount or cost arising from the facility or security not being discharged at Completion.

### B2. Bluefen change-of-control consent (~AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30% of FY26)

**Seller position:** "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours; condition satisfied on delivery of counterparty's written consent.
**Disclosure Letter:** No final written consent; no evidence the conditions in cl. 11.3 are satisfied.

**Why it's a problem:**
- This is the Company's largest customer. Losing it post-Completion would wipe out close to a third of revenue; the purchase price was presumably built on a multiple of that revenue.
- "Reasonable endeavours" is a low standard; the Seller can say it tried.
- The CP as drafted is satisfied on delivery of "written consent" — but DD-002 cl. 11.3 attaches *conditions* to consent. A conditional consent, or a consent given subject to re-pricing or termination rights, would technically satisfy the Seller's CP while leaving the Buyer exposed.
- "Addressed" is not a legal status.

**Push back:**
- CP: Bluefen's written, **unconditional** consent (or written confirmation that all 11.3 conditions are satisfied), in a form approved by the Buyer, not revocable, with no amendment to pricing or term. Seller obligation: *best* endeavours; Buyer to be kept informed and to have a right to attend/participate in discussions.
- Buyer-only waiver right; long-stop date.
- Fall-back if the Seller won't accept the CP: price adjustment / deferred consideration tied to Bluefen retention for 12 months post-Completion, plus specific indemnity for loss if Bluefen terminates or re-prices on the basis of change of control.
- Request the current status now — the letter is six weeks old.

### B3. Ironquay IP — Statement of Work 3 (AUD 180k open)

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment is "adequate."
**Disclosure Letter:** IP in SOW3 project materials only transfers on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee; DD-010 shows AUD 180k unpaid; no receipt, no confirmatory assignment on file; and the Seller volunteers that DD-010 is "not independent bank verification of non-payment" (i.e. it might be *more* unpaid, or paid — they don't know).

**Why it's a problem:**
- The issue is not the AUD 180k. The issue is that **the Company may not own the IP in whatever SOW3 built**, and we do not know what that is. If it is part of the analytics platform the Buyer is paying AUD 24m for, this is a title-to-assets problem, not a payables problem.
- An indemnity capped at the fee covers the cost of paying Ironquay, but not: the cost if Ironquay refuses to assign, raises its price, asserts licence terms, or has already licensed the materials elsewhere; business interruption; or re-development cost.
- The Seller's own drafting of cl. 12 would sweep this "existing indemnity" under the 20% cap and 18-month limit (see A2).

**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion: the Seller to pay the AUD 180k (and anything else outstanding), obtain a receipt, and deliver a **confirmatory deed of assignment** from Ironquay of all SOW1–3 project materials and IP, plus moral rights consents from Ironquay personnel — as Completion deliverables.
- Confirm in DD exactly what SOW3 delivered and whether it is in the production codebase.
- Specific indemnity (outside cap, 6 years): all loss arising from any Ironquay IP not vesting in the Company at Completion, including cost of acquiring, licensing or re-developing it.
- Extend IP warranties: Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business; no third party has any claim; all contractor IP assigned in writing.

### B4. Completion bonuses (AUD 420k) not in the funds flow

**Seller position:** "A matter for the Seller," not itemised.
**Disclosure Letter:** AUD 420k in Completion bonuses conditional on Completion and continued employment; not in the funds flow; silent on payroll tax, super and on-costs.

**Why it's a problem:**
- These are transaction bonuses **payable by the Company**, triggered by Completion. If not paid or funded at Completion, the Company (now the Buyer's) pays them. That is classic "transaction cost leakage" on a debt-free/cash-free deal.
- Payroll tax (NSW: 5.45%), superannuation (12% SG for FY27) and any related on-costs could add roughly AUD 70–75k, so the true number is closer to AUD 490–500k.
- "Continued employment" condition — if paid post-Completion, the Buyer may become the party bound to keep those employees on, or face claims if they leave.
- "A matter for the Seller" is the correct outcome, but it has to be *in the document*: an unitemised oral assurance is worth nothing.

**Push back:**
- Treat bonuses plus all on-costs as Transaction Expenses / debt-like items deducted from the price, or paid by the Seller at Completion through the funds flow with evidence.
- Specific indemnity (uncapped) for any bonus, on-cost or claim arising from DD-005 arrangements.
- Obtain the bonus letters; check who the recipients are (if they are key staff, think about retention arrangements the Buyer *does* want, separately funded).

### B5. Export / privacy incident (DD-006, ~1,240 records)

**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter," not expected to be material.
**Disclosure Letter:** Download link sent to an unintended external email address; ~1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps; unknown whether accessed; unknown scope; unknown whether notification required; investigation "preliminary" as at 22 September.

**Why it's a problem:**
- Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires assessment within 30 days of a suspected eligible data breach. The incident was disclosed as "preliminary" on 22 September; it is now 4 November. Either the assessment has been done (and the Seller should tell us the outcome) or the Company is already outside the statutory assessment window. Both matter.
- The data appears to be customer data (names/roles/activity timestamps of a B2B analytics company's users). If any of it is Bluefen's or Mossvale's data, there are likely contractual notification and security obligations under those customer contracts, and reputational/termination risk.
- Post-December 2022 amendments, maximum civil penalties for serious interference with privacy are the greater of AUD 50m, 3× benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover. "Not expected to be material" is the Seller's hope, not an assessment.
- Characterising it as "not a confirmed breach" and "no loss amount" is positioning for a later argument that the warranty was not breached and the loss was unforeseeable.

**Push back:**
- Immediate DD request: status of investigation, whether the recipient confirmed deletion/non-access, whether the OAIC or affected individuals/customers were notified, whose data it was, and copies of any legal advice (or at minimum a factual summary).
- Specific indemnity, outside cap, 6 years: all loss, fines, notification costs, remediation, customer claims and contractual consequences arising from DD-006.
- Warranty that the Company has complied with the Privacy Act and APPs and has no unnotified eligible data breaches, *not* qualified by DD-006 disclosure.
- Consider a CP or pre-Completion covenant requiring the Seller to complete the assessment and make any required notifications before Completion, with Buyer approval of communications.

### B6. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.
**Disclosure Letter:** Three *related* renewals to be read together for timing and scope; the Seller does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Why it's a problem:** Three identical AUD 110k contracts with the same supplier, to be "read together," looks like a single AUD 330k commitment split to stay under an approval or disclosure threshold. Questions: Are they signed? Are they pre-Completion commitments that bind the Company for a new term? Are the amounts accrued (debt-like) or future opex? Are they related-party in any way? Is Sandbar a necessary supplier?

**Push back:** Get the three documents and the commercial rationale. If renewals were entered into after the locked-box date / outside the ordinary course, treat as leakage. Pre-Completion conduct covenant: no new or renewed commitments above a threshold (say AUD 50k) without Buyer consent, and no splitting of commitments. If the Buyer does not need Sandbar, require termination pre-Completion or price adjustment.

### B7. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)

- **Lease:** The Seller says it is a "notification" not a consent. Fine — but then the notification should be given pre-Completion and evidence delivered at Completion. Confirm landlord has not objected and the lease has no change-of-control termination right.
- **Mossvale:** The letter says restriction on assignment, not consent on share sale. Accept provisionally, but verify the clause ourselves (change-of-control clauses are often drafted as "assignment includes change in control"). Warranty that no customer or supplier contract contains a change-of-control right other than as disclosed, with a list.

### B8. Title (DD-012)

**Seller position:** Title evidenced by the Company's own share register.
**Disclosure Letter:** The register is "the source relied on"; Buyer has not completed its own verification.

**Why it's a problem:** A company's share register is maintained by the company (i.e. by the Seller's own people). It is evidence of registration, not of beneficial ownership or absence of encumbrances. The Seller is simultaneously (i) relying on this as the sole title evidence and (ii) seeking to cap the title warranty at 20% and 18 months (A1). We should not accept both.

**Push back:** ASIC extract; PPSR search against the Company and the Seller (for security over the shares — Riverlark may have a share mortgage); share certificates; copies of any shareholder agreements, options, convertible notes, employee equity. Fundamental warranties on title: legal and beneficial owner, free of all Encumbrances, no options or rights to subscribe. Uncapped, 6 years (per A1).

### B9. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

Not acceptable. Tax: separate uncapped (or price-capped) tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, with a claim period tied to the ATO amendment period; the Seller controls nothing after Completion. IP: given Ironquay (B3), IP warranties need to be at least a higher cap and longer period (3–4 years), and the ownership warranty should sit with fundamentals.

---

## Part C – Points of general positioning

- **Stale date.** All disclosures speak at 22 September 2026. Require updated disclosure now and a formal bring-down at Completion. Any deterioration between now and Completion is for the Seller.
- **Non-reliance (20.5).** Non-reliance on representations outside the SPA is standard; non-reliance that extends to the warranties themselves, or that purports to exclude liability for misleading conduct under the ACL/ASIC Act for fraud, is not. Limit to pre-contractual statements and carve out fraud and non-excludable statutory liability.
- **Exclusive remedy (12.8).** Acceptable for general warranty damages. Must not exclude: rescission for fraud, specific performance of Completion obligations, injunctive relief, the price-adjustment and leakage mechanics, or statutory rights that cannot be excluded.
- **Retention / escrow.** Given the number of unresolved items and a Seller that wants post-Completion "releases" and "reasonable endeavours," a retention of **AUD 2.4–3.6m (10–15%)** held for 18–24 months is justified, releasable against resolution of Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-006 and Bluefen. If the Seller resists on the basis that it is a clean-skin seller, the alternative is to fix every item pre-Completion as CPs/deliverables.
- **Seller covenant strength.** Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd — a "Ventures" vehicle may distribute proceeds immediately post-Completion. Diligence its covenant; consider a parent guarantee or the retention above. A good indemnity against an empty shell is worth nothing.
- **W&I insurance.** If the Seller's attitude to caps is immovable, W&I could bridge the gap on the general warranty book — but insurers will exclude all the known matters in Part B. Those still need specific indemnities or price fixes from the Seller.

---

## Summary of recommendations (priority order)

| # | Issue | Recommended Buyer position |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Riverlark AUD 3.2m facility** | Repay and deliver signed release / PPSR discharge **at** Completion via funds flow and payout letter; dollar-for-dollar price deduction for any debt remaining; uncapped indemnity. Not post-Completion. |
| 2 | **Fundamental / title warranties** | Carve out of cl. 12 entirely. Cap at 100% of price; 6 years; no basket/de minimis. Title evidence: ASIC, PPSR (Company and Seller), certificates, cap table docs — not just the register. |
| 3 | **"All Claims of any nature" drafting (12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5)** | Reverse the default: limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims. Express carve-outs for fundamentals, tax, specific indemnities, leakage, completion obligations, fraud, non-excludable statutory liability. |
| 4 | **Bluefen consent** | CP: unconditional written consent in Buyer-approved form, with 11.3 conditions satisfied; best endeavours; Buyer-only waiver. Fallback: deferred consideration / indemnity tied to retention. Confirm current status. |
| 5 | **Cl. 8.3 Buyer knowledge + general data-room disclosure** | Delete constructive/"discoverable" knowledge and adviser imputation; actual knowledge of named individuals only, and only of fairly disclosed matters. Replace blanket disclosure with fair-disclosure standard and specifically referenced documents. Strike or neutralise DL [1.4]. Bring-down disclosure letter with no new disclosures against warranties. |
| 6 | **Ironquay SOW3 IP** | Seller pays all outstanding fees and delivers confirmatory assignment + moral rights consents as Completion deliverables; uncapped specific indemnity for IP not vesting; confirm what SOW3 built. |
| 7 | **DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs ≈ AUD 490–500k)** | Treat as transaction expense/debt-like item deducted from price or paid by Seller through the funds flow with evidence; uncapped indemnity. |
| 8 | **DD-006 privacy incident** | Immediate status update (NDB assessment window has likely run); specific uncapped indemnity, 6 years; unqualified privacy-compliance warranty; pre-Completion covenant to complete assessment and notifications with Buyer sign-off. |
| 9 | **Tax / IP regimes** | Separate tax indemnity (price-capped or uncapped, ATO amendment period + buffer). IP warranties: higher cap, 3–4 years; ownership with fundamentals. |
| 10 | **General regime numbers** | Tipping basket at ~1% (not deductible); general claims period 24 months; 20% cap acceptable only if known matters sit outside it — otherwise 30–40% or retention. |
| 11 | **Sandbar renewals** | Obtain documents; treat as leakage if outside ordinary course/post-locked-box; pre-Completion conduct covenant with AUD 50k threshold and anti-splitting language. |
| 12 | **Lease / Mossvale** | Notification given pre-Completion with evidence; verify Mossvale clause ourselves; warranty listing all change-of-control provisions. |
| 13 | **Retention / covenant** | 10–15% retention for 18–24 months released against resolution of items 1, 4, 6, 8; diligence Seller covenant strength; consider guarantee. W&I only as a supplement, not a substitute, for the known issues. |
| 14 | **Timing** | Require refreshed disclosure immediately (current letter is six weeks stale) and formal bring-down at Completion. |

**Overall negotiating posture:** The Seller's package offers general-warranty-level protection for fundamental-level risks, and asks the Buyer to inherit ~AUD 3.6m of debt and bonus leakage on a debt-free/cash-free price, plus unresolved IP title and privacy exposure, with an 18-month, 20%-capped claim as the only recourse. Our mark-up should re-separate fundamentals, indemnities and tax from the general regime, convert every "to be provided after Completion" into a Completion deliverable or price deduction, and replace blanket disclosure with fair disclosure. These are not aggressive positions; they are the ordinary allocation of known risks to the party that created them and controls their resolution.

Happy to turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up of the SPA and a response letter to Seller's counsel, and to draft the DD requisition list (Bluefen status, Riverlark payout letter, Ironquay deliverables, bonus letters, DD-006 investigation outcome, Sandbar contracts, PPSR/ASIC searches).
